Is there an environmental Kuznets curve in Saudi Arabia? cointegration and decoupling evidence

  • SM

    Saqib Muneer 1*

  • MH

    Mazhar Hussain Choudhary 1

  • GD

    Ghulam Dastgeer 2

  • SA

    Shaikh Aftab Ahmed 1

  • MU

    Mueen Uddin 3

  • 1. Department of Economics and Finance, College of Business Administration, University of Ha’il, Ha’il, Saudi Arabia

  • 2. Department of Management and Information Systems, College of Business Administration, University of Ha’il, Ha’il, Saudi Arabia

  • 3. College of Computing and Information Technology, University of Doha for Science and Technology, Doha, Qatar

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

Introduction:

This study asks whether the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) describes the relationship between income and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in Saudi Arabia.

Methods:

A log-quadratic EKC specification, augmented with primary energy use and the renewable share of primary energy, is estimated on annual data for 1990–2022 (n = 33; 31 effective observations in the dynamic models). The sample ends in 2022 because the harmonised real-income series ends in that year; data for 2023–2024 are used descriptively only. The autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds test provides the decisive evidence. For the specification selected by both the Akaike and Schwarz criteria, ARDL(2,0,0,0,1), the bounds F-statistic is 2.01, below the 10% lower (I(0)) bound of both the asymptotic (2.45) and finite-sample (2.75) critical values. It remains below the I(0) bound in all 162 lag configurations, in the best-fitting configuration free of residual serial correlation, after adding level shifts for 2014 and 2016, and after adding oil rents and trade openness. A Gregory–Hansen test allowing a regime shift also detects no cointegration. Unit-root tests indicate that per-capita emissions are stationary around a shifting mean, whereas income is integrated of order one. Long-run coefficients from the ARDL, nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) and dynamic ordinary least squares (DOLS) models are therefore reported only as exploratory quantities with measures of uncertainty. The income terms are jointly insignificant in every specification, and the Lind–Mehlum slope conditions for an inverted U are not met. The NARDL Wald test does not reject long-run income symmetry (p = 0.62), a result conditional on a long-run framework that the bounds test does not support.

Results:

The data provide no evidence of an inverted-U EKC, but they also do not establish a statistically significant U-shape. Total emissions show relative but not absolute decoupling from gross domestic product (GDP): the Tapio elasticity is 0.34 for 2016–2022, and total emissions rose by 7.9% between 2016 and 2024. The decline in carbon intensity slowed after 2016.

Discussion:

These patterns are described as associations and are not attributed causally to Vision 2030. Code and data that reproduce every table and figure are provided.

1 Introduction

Whether economic growth can continue without a commensurate rise in greenhouse-gas emissions is a central question for hydrocarbon-exporting economies as the international community moves towards mid-century net-zero targets. The workhorse framework for this question is the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC), which hypothesises that pollution first rises with income and then declines once income passes a threshold, tracing an inverted U (Grossman and Krueger, 1995). The framework, and related STIRPAT-type (Stochastic Impacts by Regression on Population, Affluence and Technology) analyses, have been applied across sectors and regions, including transport emissions in South Africa (Oladunni and Olanrewaju, 2022; Oladunni et al., 2024). Its application to hydrocarbon exporters is problematic. Where hydrocarbon export revenue constitutes a large share of gross domestic product (GDP), income is mechanically tied to fossil-fuel extraction and, through subsidised domestic energy, to fossil-fuel combustion. Saudi Arabia exemplifies the case: it is among the world’s largest oil exporters and records some of the highest per capita carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in the world (Friedlingstein et al., 2026). Its Vision 2030 programme aims to diversify the economy away from petroleum, and the credibility of that programme depends in part on whether growth can be decoupled from emissions (Al-Saidi, 2022; Amran et al., 2020).

A sizeable literature has estimated the income–emissions relationship for Saudi Arabia (e.g., Alajlan and Alreshaidi, 2022). Table 1 summarises the principal single-country studies by sample period, dependent variable, regressors, estimator, treatment of cointegration and structural breaks, and principal EKC result. Three regularities emerge. First, the evidence on the EKC is mixed rather than uniform. Seven of the twelve studies find no inverted U (Alkhathlan and Javid, 2015; Alshehry and Belloumi, 2017; Samargandi, 2017; Raggad, 2018; 2020; Aldegheishem, 2024; Moustafa and Alomran, 2025); six of these rely mainly on autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) or nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) estimation, and three (Raggad, 2020; Aldegheishem, 2024; Moustafa and Alomran, 2025) do not include a quadratic income term. By contrast, studies using simultaneous-equation or Johansen/vector error-correction model (VECM) approaches report an inverted U, either for aggregate CO2 (Kahia et al., 2021b; Alsaedi et al., 2022) or only for liquid-fuel emissions (Kahia et al., 2021a). Second, every study in Table 1 that reports a cointegration test concludes, on at least one test, that a long-run relationship exists, and long-run elasticities are then interpreted as equilibrium parameters. To our knowledge, none of these studies tests for the degenerate case in which the dependent variable is itself stationary. Third, only four of the twelve studies model structural breaks: three at the unit-root stage (Alshehry and Belloumi, 2017; Raggad, 2018; 2020) and two in the long-run equation itself, through impulse-indicator saturation dummies (Raggad, 2018) or intervention dummies in a structural time-series model (Alkhathlan and Javid, 2015).

Related sector-level research has already examined two aspects of the question elsewhere: the shape of the income–emissions curve for transport greenhouse-gas emissions in South Africa (Oladunni et al., 2024) and the fossil-energy, urbanisation and passenger-vehicle channels of emissions mitigation, analysed with system-econometric methods (Oladunni et al., 2025a; 2025b). What remains to be examined, particularly for a hydrocarbon exporter, is whether a stable levels relationship between income and emissions exists before the shape of that relationship is interpreted. This study addresses that question, which corresponds to the second and third regularities. Its contribution is methodological and empirical rather than a claim to a new theory. Methodologically, the paper treats cointegration as a hypothesis to be tested, with a decision rule fixed in advance: no estimate is interpreted as a long-run equilibrium parameter unless both the bounds F- and t-statistics lie beyond their I (1) critical bounds. The decision is assessed against asymptotic critical values and against finite-sample critical values simulated for the exact design (T = 33 with 31 effective observations, four regressors and the selected lag structure). It is also checked with an F-test on the lagged regressors that detects the degenerate case of a stationary dependent variable (McNown et al., 2018), across the full lag grid, after allowing for a regime shift, and after adding omitted structural variables. Empirically, the paper shows that the statistical properties of the data explain why a stable levels relationship is not found. Per-capita emissions are stationary around a shifting mean, whereas real income is integrated of order one, I (1), so a common stochastic trend is implausible. The paper also replaces the qualitative decoupling discussion common in this literature with explicit decoupling metrics and a formal test for a post-2016 change in the carbon-intensity trend. All data are public, and code that regenerates every table and figure accompanies the paper.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature and sets out the conceptual framework and hypotheses. Section 3 describes the data and estimation strategy. Section 4 reports the results. Section 5 discusses them, and Section 6 concludes.

2 Literature review and conceptual framework

2.1 The environmental Kuznets curve and its discontents

The EKC hypothesis posits an inverted-U relationship between per capita GDP and environmental damage: pollution rises with output at low levels of development, peaks at a turning point, and declines thereafter as structural change towards services, cleaner technology, and stronger regulation takes hold (Grossman and Krueger, 1995). Its empirical support varies with the country studied, the pollutant, the period, and the method. Cross-national studies show that the inverted U is far from universal (Shuai et al., 2017; Thio et al., 2022), and single-country evidence shows that it can disappear once energy consumption, trade, and structural variables are controlled for (Farhani and Ozturk, 2015). For CO2 in particular, a globally mixed pollutant with no local damage signal, turning points are often statistically insignificant or lie outside the observed income range (Farhani and Ozturk, 2015; Saidi and Ben Mbarek, 2017). A further statistical point is often overlooked: a positive linear and a negative quadratic coefficient are necessary but not sufficient for an inverted U. The slope of the fitted relationship must also be significantly positive at the lower end and significantly negative at the upper end of the observed income range (Lind and Mehlum, 2010). Sector-level applications show that even where the EKC is supported, economies may remain on its rising segment: for transport emissions in South Africa, all nine provinces are still below the turning point (Oladunni et al., 2024).

2.2 STIRPAT and the IPAT tradition

A more structural approach to anthropogenic environmental impact is provided by IPAT (impact = population × affluence × technology) and its stochastic generalisation STIRPAT, which express impact as a function of population, affluence, and technology (Dietz and Rosa, 1997; York et al., 2003). The framework nests the EKC when a squared affluence term is added, so that the two income terms represent affluence and its square, and it disciplines the specification with demographic and technology channels (Fan et al., 2006). Applications typically find affluence and energy or carbon intensity to be the dominant drivers, with the roles of population and urbanisation varying across settings (Lv et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023; Lee and Zhao, 2023; Oladunni and Olanrewaju, 2022). The STIRPAT literature has increasingly adopted time-series cointegration estimators (Pattak et al., 2023), panel methods (Ghazali and Ali, 2019) and system-econometric approaches to fossil-energy use and emissions mitigation (Oladunni et al., 2025a).

In this paper STIRPAT is used as an organising framework, not as a fully specified structural model. Two features of the specification depart from a complete STIRPAT model and are stated explicitly. First, population does not enter as a separate regressor. Expressing emissions and income in per capita terms imposes a unit elasticity of total emissions with respect to population, and Section 3.1 explains why a free population elasticity cannot be estimated reliably in this sample. Second, technology is represented by only two proxies: energy use per capita, which, conditional on income, captures energy intensity, and the renewable share, which captures the fuel mix. The model is therefore a parsimonious STIRPAT-type specification that conditions the EKC income terms on the two proximate technology channels.

2.3 Energy, oil rents, and the carbon curse in rentier economies

In oil-exporting states the relationship between income and emissions is shaped by a distinctive political economy. The “carbon curse” hypothesis holds that resource-abundant countries develop production structures that favour energy- and carbon-intensive activities, keep domestic energy prices low, and provide weak incentives for efficiency. As a result, emissions intensity tends to rise with resource dependence (Nwani et al., 2024; Okere et al., 2026). Rents from oil and gas exports have been found to be positively related to emissions levels in panels of Middle East and North Africa and other oil-rich countries, while the magnitude of this relationship varies with institutional quality and the degree of dependence (Dabboussi, 2024; Mahmood et al., 2023; Abd El Nasser et al., 2025). Some studies identify thresholds of rent dependence beyond which the carbon curse becomes active (Nwani et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Commodity-price volatility is a further channel: changes in world oil prices alter rent revenues and, through rent-financed spending and administered prices, domestic energy demand (Liu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). A complete model of Saudi emissions would therefore include rents. Section 4.6 adds oil rents and trade openness to the baseline specification as a robustness check.

2.4 Evidence for Saudi Arabia

Table 1 shows that the Saudi evidence is less uniform than is often stated. ARDL-based studies of transport emissions (Alshehry and Belloumi, 2017), sectoral value added (Samargandi, 2017), urbanisation (Raggad, 2018) and air transport and trade (Aldegheishem, 2024) generally find a positive, monotonic long-run association between income and emissions and do not support an inverted U, although Aldegheishem (2024) includes no quadratic income term. By contrast, Kahia et al. (2021b) and Alsaedi et al. (2022) report an inverted U using simultaneous-equation and VECM frameworks, and Kahia et al. (2021a) find one only for liquid-fuel emissions. Energy consumption is the most consistently significant proximate driver, and renewable energy has so far been too small to offset the emissions associated with growth (Kahia et al., 2021a; 2021b). Studies of asymmetry differ in the direction of the asymmetry they report. Raggad (2020) and Toumi and Toumi (2019) report asymmetric responses, Moustafa and Alomran (2025) report reductions in emissions after positive growth shocks, and, outside the Adebayo et al., 2021 find long-run asymmetry in a NARDL model for Chile, with income decreases having a larger effect on consumption-based emissions than income increases. Every study in Table 1 that reports a cointegration test finds a long-run relationship on at least one test. This uniformity is itself notable, given the low power and size distortions of cointegration tests in samples of 25–55 annual observations.

2.5 Determinants beyond income: trade, finance, and urbanisation

Other determinants of emissions include trade openness, whose effect depends on whether scale or composition effects dominate (Li and Haneklaus, 2022; Udeagha and Breitenbach, 2023; Zhou et al., 2025). Financial development may ease funding for clean investment or accelerate energy-intensive activity (Ali et al., 2019; Shoaib et al., 2020; Nurgazina et al., 2021). Urbanisation raises energy demand through agglomeration but can lower it through density-related efficiency (Sharif et al., 2026), and vehicle ownership is an important urban channel in transport-emissions studies (Oladunni and Olanrewaju, 2022). Oladunni et al. (2025b) examine the joint impacts of urbanisation and passenger vehicles on carbon emissions in Gauteng, South Africa, with system-econometric methods. Omitting these variables from a parsimonious model is a potential source of misspecification. This paper does not infer their role from residual diagnostics alone. Instead, it adds the two most closely linked to the rentier and trade channels discussed above, oil rents and trade openness, and tests their effect directly (Section 4.6).

2.6 Methodological lessons: cointegration as a question, not an assumption

In much of the applied EKC literature, including the Saudi studies, the cointegration test functions as a procedural step. Once a significant bounds statistic is obtained, long-run elasticities are estimated without examining how fragile, sample-dependent or specification-dependent the levels relationship is. Three methodological points follow. First, the bounds test has low power in samples of about 30 annual observations, and tests based on asymptotic critical values can be over-sized; finite-sample critical values (Narayan, 2005) or simulated values should therefore be reported. Second, a significant negative error-correction coefficient does not establish cointegration. When the dependent variable is itself stationary, the coefficient on its lag will tend to be negative and significant even if the regressors are unrelated to it. This degenerate case is detected by also testing the lagged regressors (McNown et al., 2018). Third, single-equation long-run estimators such as dynamic ordinary least squares (DOLS; Stock and Watson, 1993) presuppose cointegration and cannot be used to confirm it. In this paper they serve only to check whether the sign pattern of the income terms depends on the estimator.

2.7 Conceptual framework and hypotheses

Figure 1 summarises the framework. Affluence, represented by centred log income and its square, acts on per capita emissions through scale and composition effects. Energy use per capita represents the technique channel, and the renewable share represents fuel substitution. Population enters only through the per capita normalisation. The omitted structural drivers (oil rents, trade, financial development and subsidised energy prices) are expected to affect both income and emissions. Two of them, oil rents and trade openness, are added in robustness checks rather than in the baseline model because of the degrees-of-freedom constraint; financial development and energy prices are discussed but not modelled. The parsimonious specification is also defensible on theoretical grounds. The EKC is a reduced-form relationship in which scale, composition and technique effects operate through the proximate determinants of emissions, namely, income, the energy intensity of activity and the fuel mix (Grossman and Krueger, 1995; York et al., 2003). Rents, trade and financial development act on emissions largely through these proximate channels, so omitting them biases the income coefficients only to the extent that they affect emissions other than through energy use and the fuel mix. Section 4.6 tests this possibility directly. The four hypotheses are stated in testable form together with their statistical decision rules.

FIGURE 1

2.7.1 H1 (inverted-U EKC)

H0: β1 = β2 = 0 (Wald test) on the income terms, tested in the static bivariate log-quadratic relationship (Equation 1 without lnEN and REN), in the conditional long-run coefficients of the ARDL models (λ1 and λ2, Equation 4) and in DOLS (Equation 8). An inverted U is supported only if (i) β2 < 0 (because income is centred, the sign of β1 only locates the turning point relative to mean log income); (ii) the implied turning point lies inside the observed income range; and (iii) the Lind and Mehlum (2010) slope conditions hold, that is, the slope β1 + 2β2x is significantly positive at the minimum and significantly negative at the maximum of the observed (centred) income, x, at the 5% level.

2.7.2 H2 (levels relationship)

In Equation 3, H0f: φ = θ1 = … = θk = 0 (bounds F-test) and H0f: φ = 0 (bounds t-test). A levels relationship is accepted only if, at the 5% level, the F-statistic exceeds its I (1) upper bound and the t-statistic is more negative than its I (1) bound, under both the asymptotic critical values (Pesaran et al., 2001) and the finite-sample critical values simulated for this design. If the F-statistic is below its I (0) bound, or the t-statistic is less negative than its I (0) bound, H2 is not supported; values between the bounds are inconclusive. The F-test on the lagged regressors alone, H0: θ1 = … = θk = 0 (McNown et al., 2018), is reported to identify the degenerate case.

2.7.3 H3 (asymmetry)

In the NARDL model of Equation 7, H0: θ+ = θ− (long-run symmetry) and H0: δ+ = δ− (impact symmetry), each tested with a Wald F-test at the 5% level. Because the long-run symmetry test is meaningful only if a long-run relationship exists, the H3 decision is conditional on H2.

2.7.4 H4 (decoupling after 2016)

Decoupling is measured with the Tapio (2005) elasticity ε = (%ΔCO2)/(%ΔGDP) for total emissions and total real GDP over 2016–2022 (Equation 9). Absolute (strong) decoupling requires ε < 0 with positive GDP growth; relative (weak) decoupling requires 0 ≤ ε < 0.8. In addition, the change in the carbon-intensity trend after 2016, κ2 in Equation 10, is tested with H0: κ2 = 0; an acceleration of the decline would require κ2 < 0. H4 is supported only if total emissions decoupled absolutely. Even then, the result would be described as consistent with, rather than caused by, Vision 2030, because the design contains no policy-evaluation identification strategy.

3 Data and methodology

3.1 Data, sample and variables

The study uses annual data for Saudi Arabia from Our World in Data (OWID), which harmonises primary sources in two public repositories: the OWID CO2 dataset (github.com/owid/co2-data) and the OWID energy dataset (github.com/owid/energy-data). Both were accessed on 11 October 2026. Territorial fossil CO2 emissions come from the Global Carbon Budget (Friedlingstein et al., 2026). Primary energy use and the renewable share come from the Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy (Energy Institute, 2025). Total real GDP comes from the Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden, 2025), and population from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 (WPP; United Nations, 2024), which incorporates the downward revision of Saudi population estimates that followed the 2022 census. Per-capita GDP, emissions and energy use are all expressed relative to this population series. Oil rents and trade openness for the robustness models are taken from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI; World Bank, 2026). Table 2 lists every variable with its definition, unit, transformation, source, coverage and the observations used in estimation.

Variable definitions, transformations, sources and coverage.

Dynamic models lose two initial observations, so ARDL, NARDL, and first-difference models use 31 observations (1992–2022); DOLS, and the models augmented with oil rents and trade use 30 (1992–2021). The years 2023–2024 are used descriptively only.

The emissions, energy and renewable-share series are complete for 1990–2024, but the real GDP series ends in 2022 in the source database. Every model that contains income is therefore estimated on 1990–2022 (33 annual observations; 31 effective observations after two initial observations are lost to the lag structure). The years 2023 and 2024 are used only descriptively: in the trajectories and renewable shares shown in Sections 4.1 and 4.7, and in the 2016–2024 growth rates of total and per capita emissions reported in Section 4.7. They cannot enter any econometric model because no harmonised income observation exists for them, and splicing income from a different source would introduce a level break at the junction. World Bank oil rents end in 2021, so models that include rents are estimated on 1990–2021. With 31 effective observations, the preferred ARDL leaves 23 residual degrees of freedom and the common-lag ARDL and NARDL leave 20, so the cointegration, asymmetry and break tests have low power, and null results should be read as non-detection rather than as evidence of absence.

The dependent variable is the natural logarithm of CO2 emissions per capita (lnCO2). Income enters as centred log real GDP per capita, xt = lnGDPt − m̄, where m̄ = 10.544 is the 1990–2022 sample mean of ln real GDP per capita. The quadratic term is the square of the centred variable, lnGDP2t ≡ xt2 = (lnGDPt − m̄)2. Centring reduces collinearity between the two income terms and changes neither the fitted curve nor the significance of the quadratic coefficient; it does change the interpretation of β1, which is the income elasticity at the sample mean of log income (geometric-mean income of about 37,960 international dollars, Int$, at 2011 prices). Energy use enters as lnEN, the log of primary energy consumption per capita, so its coefficient is an elasticity. The renewable share, REN, enters in levels, in percentage points, because it equals zero in 1990–2010 and cannot be logged. Its coefficient is therefore a semi-elasticity: 100 × β4 is the approximate percentage change in per capita emissions associated with a one-percentage-point increase in the renewable share. Because REN never exceeds 0.157% of primary energy in the estimation sample, a one-percentage-point change lies far outside the data, and the magnitude of the coefficient should not be interpreted economically.

Population is not included as a separate regressor, for three reasons. First, the per capita formulation already imposes a unit population elasticity on total emissions. Second, the integration order of log population is ambiguous (Supplementary Appendix Table A1). With a constant and up to three lags, the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test rejects a unit root in the first difference (p = 0.004), but the Phillips–Perron (PP) test does not (p = 0.471) and the Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin (KPSS) test rejects stationarity of the first difference (p = 0.025). All three tests indicate that the second difference is stationary. Because the bounds procedure is invalid if any regressor is I (2), including a series that may be I (2) would compromise the central test. Third, the Saudi population series contains an absolute decline between 2017 and 2018 (30.78–30.37 million) that coincides with the departure of expatriate workers. A free population elasticity estimated from 33 observations would largely reflect this episode rather than a structural demographic effect.

3.2 Model specification

The empirical model embeds the EKC income terms within a parsimonious STIRPAT-type specification:where β0 is the intercept, β1 is the income elasticity at mean income, β2 is the curvature parameter, β3 is the energy elasticity, β4 is the renewable-share semi-elasticity and ut is the error term. An inverted U requires β2 < 0, with the turning point inside the observed income range; because income is centred, β1 is the slope at mean log income, and its sign only indicates whether the turning point lies above or below that mean. The slope of the income–emissions relationship and its turning point are given in Equation 2.so the turning point is expressed in uncentred income units by adding back m̄. Standard errors for x* are obtained by the delta method. The Lind–Mehlum conditions are evaluated as s (xmᵢn) and s (xmax) at the observed extremes, xmᵢn = −0.562 and xmax = 0.401, which correspond to Int$21,637 and Int$56,686.

3.3 Estimation strategy

The estimation strategy proceeds in six steps.

  • Step 1: integration order. Each series is tested with the ADF (Dickey and Fuller, 1979), PP (Phillips and Perron, 1988) and KPSS (Kwiatkowski et al., 1992) tests, with a constant and, as a robustness check, a constant and trend. ADF lags are selected by the Akaike information criterion (AIC) up to a maximum of three, using the rule ⌊4 (T/100)^0.25⌋ = 3 for T = 33. The PP test uses a Newey–West (Bartlett) bandwidth of three, and the KPSS bandwidth is selected automatically. Zivot and Andrews (1992) tests with an endogenous intercept break (model A, which includes a trend) check whether apparent unit roots reflect unmodelled shifts.

  • Step 2: levels relationship. The conditional error-correction form of an ARDL (p, q1, … , qk) model under Pesaran et al. (2001) Case III (unrestricted intercept, no trend) is

Parameter constancy is assessed with cumulative sum (CUSUM) and CUSUM-of-squares tests of recursive residuals (Brown et al., 1975), with 5% bounds. 3.4 Reproducibility

Every estimated statistic, results table and figure is generated by code directly from the public source files; Tables 1 and 2, which summarise the literature and the variable definitions, and the summary of hypothesis decisions in Section 4.8 are compiled from these sources and outputs. The supplementary material contains the extracted dataset (Supplementary Data S1, with each variable, its source identifier and transformation), the Python code used for all estimation and figures (Supplementary Code S1; Python 3.13 with numpy 2.5, pandas 3.0, statsmodels 0.15, arch 8.0 and matplotlib 3.11), the simulated critical values with their random seeds, and the complete model output. Running the code reproduces every statistic to the printed precision.

4 Results

4.1 Descriptive statistics and trends

Table 3 summarises the estimation sample. Mean per capita CO2 emissions over 1990–2022 are 20.33 t, ranging between 14.67 t (1998) and 24.37 t (1993). Real GDP per capita rose roughly 2.6-fold, from about Int$21,600 in 1990 to about Int$56,700 in 2022 (2011 prices). Energy use per capita is high and only moderately trending. The renewable share is negligible for almost the entire sample (mean 0.011%), reaching 0.16% in 2022 and, in the descriptive extension of the series, 0.36% in 2023 and 0.73% in 2024 (Section 4.7). Figure 2 shows the central empirical fact of the paper: between 1990 and 2022 income per capita grew by about 160%, whereas per capita emissions fluctuated around a nearly flat level after the early 1990s, and energy use drifted up only modestly.

4.2 Unit-root tests

Table 4

reports the ADF, PP and KPSS statistics, p-values and lag or bandwidth choices for each variable in levels and first differences. The results are as follows.

  • lnGDP and lnEN are I (1). All three tests indicate a unit root in levels and stationarity in first differences.

  • lnCO2 is stationary in levels. ADF (p = 0.013) and PP (p = 0.041) reject the unit root, and KPSS does not reject stationarity (p = 0.236). With a trend, ADF still rejects (p = 0.005), PP does not (p = 0.162), and KPSS does not reject trend-stationarity (Supplementary Appendix Table A2). Allowing for an endogenous break, the Zivot–Andrews statistic is −5.70, with a level shift from 1997, which exceeds the 1% critical value of −5.34 in absolute value (Section 4.6). On balance, per capita emissions are best described as stationary around a mean that shifted in the late 1990s.

  • The centred quadratic income term, lnGDP2, is stationary in levels by all three tests with a constant (with a trend, KPSS rejects stationarity; Supplementary Appendix Table A2).

  • REN is not stationary in levels. In differences the evidence is mixed: PP rejects the unit root (p = 0.002), KPSS does not reject stationarity at 5% (p = 0.053), and ADF does not reject (p = 0.265). REN is treated as I (1).

No variable is clearly I (2) (for ΔREN, the PP test rejects a unit root), so the precondition of the bounds procedure is not violated. The integration evidence also has a substantive implication. A stationary dependent variable cannot share a common stochastic trend with an I (1) income series. In a balanced levels regression, the long-run coefficients on I (1) regressors should therefore be close to zero, and a negative coefficient on the lagged dependent variable reflects mean reversion of emissions rather than error correction towards an equilibrium with income.

4.3 Bounds tests for a levels relationship

Table 5 reports the bounds statistics for the preferred ARDL (2,0,0,0,1), the common-lag ARDL (2,1,1,1,1) and a set of alternative specifications, together with asymptotic and simulated finite-sample critical values. The F-test result is clear. For the preferred model, F = 2.01, which is below the I (0) lower bound at every conventional level under both the asymptotic critical values (10%: 2.45) and the simulated finite-sample critical values (10%: 2.75). It is also below the finite-sample I (0) bound tabulated by Narayan (2005) for n = 30, k = 4 and Case III (10%: 2.75), which our simulated values closely reproduce. The F-test on the lagged regressors alone is 1.22, below its simulated 10% I (0) bound of 2.22. The lagged regressors are therefore jointly insignificant. Together with the stationarity of lnCO2 (Section 4.2), this pattern resembles the degenerate case discussed by McNown et al. (2018), in which a significant coefficient on the lagged dependent variable reflects the dynamics of emissions alone.

The error-correction coefficient requires careful interpretation. In the preferred model φ = −0.414 (standard error, SE, 0.155; t = −2.68). The coefficient is negative, which is the sign implied by the stable error-correction representation in Equation 3, and it would be significant against a conventional t distribution (p = 0.013). The relevant benchmark, however, is the bounds t-test. The statistic lies between the I (0) and I (1) bounds at 10% (asymptotic −2.57 and −3.66; simulated −2.54 and −3.60) and above the I (0) bound at 5% (asymptotic −2.86; simulated −2.90). The t-test is therefore inconclusive at 10% and does not reject at 5%. Combined with the F-test, which falls below the I (0) bound, there is no statistical support for a levels relationship. Given the stationarity of lnCO2 (Section 4.2), the negative φ is best read as mean reversion of emissions. It does not imply that roughly 41% of a disequilibrium with income is corrected each year, and no such convergence claim is made. In the common-lag ARDL (2,1,1,1,1), φ = −0.390 (SE 0.164, t = −2.38) and F = 1.95, which lead to the same conclusion. φ is negative in every ARDL and NARDL model reported in this paper and in all 162 configurations of the lag grid (range −0.489 to −0.239).

The conclusion holds across all the specifications examined. Across all 162 lag configurations in the AIC grid, the bounds F-statistic ranges from 0.81 to 2.08 and never reaches the asymptotic 10% I (0) bound. Of these configurations, 85 show no residual serial correlation at one or two lags (Breusch–Godfrey LM and F p > 0.05); the best of them by AIC, ARDL (1,0,0,0,0), gives F = 1.17 and t = −1.99, both inside the no-rejection region (Table 5, row (j)). The conclusion therefore does not depend on the residual autocorrelation found in the preferred model. The F-statistic of the preferred model also remains below the I (0) bound after adding level shifts for 2014 and 2016 (F = 1.64), after adding oil rents (F = 1.48), and after adding oil rents and trade openness (F = 1.24). The only configuration in which F enters the inconclusive band is an ARDL with three lags of the dependent variable (F = 3.49). That model lies outside the pre-specified lag grid and shows significant residual autocorrelation at two lags (Breusch–Godfrey F = 5.34, p = 0.017), and even there F is below the 5% I (1) bound under both the asymptotic (4.01) and simulated (5.05) critical values. H2 is therefore not supported: the bounds test provides no statistical evidence of a levels relationship among emissions, income, energy use and the renewable share. In line with the decision rule of Section 2.7, none of the long-run estimates reported below is interpreted as an equilibrium elasticity.

4.4 Conditional long-run estimates and the EKC

Table 6 reports the conditional long-run coefficients implied by Equation 4 for both ARDL specifications, with delta-method standard errors, 95% confidence intervals and HAC-based p-values, together with all short-run coefficients. These estimates are exploratory: they describe the levels terms of a model in which no levels relationship has been established. Three results stand out. First, no long-run coefficient is statistically significant under conventional standard errors. The confidence intervals are very wide; for example, the interval for the energy coefficient in the common-lag model runs from −7.09 to 4.52. The one exception under HAC standard errors is REN in the preferred model (p = 0.042), which is not robust to the alternative specification (p = 0.547) and reflects the issue discussed in Section 4.5. Second, the income terms are jointly insignificant in both models: F (2, 23) = 0.01, p = 0.989, and F (2, 20) = 0.42, p = 0.660. Third, both point estimates of the quadratic coefficient are positive (0.128 and 1.511). This is the opposite of the curvature required for an inverted U, but because neither estimate is significant, it does not establish a U-shape either.

Table 7 tests H1 formally. In the descriptive bivariate log-quadratic fit shown in Figure 3, β1 = 0.144 (p = 0.129) and β2 = 0.306 (p = 0.321), and the income terms are jointly insignificant (p = 0.161). The implied turning point is a minimum, not a maximum, at about Int$30,014. It lies inside the observed income range but has a wide 95% confidence interval (Int$16,962–53,110). The Lind–Mehlum slope conditions point in the direction opposite to an inverted U: the slope is −0.20 at minimum income (p = 0.585) and +0.39 at maximum income (p = 0.130), and neither is significant. In the ARDL long-run estimates, the turning point implied by the common-lag model is also a minimum (about Int$31,223; delta-method 95% interval Int$23,990–40,637). Because this interval is conditional on a curvature coefficient that is itself insignificant (p = 0.422), it is not informative about the existence of a turning point. In the preferred model the turning point is not meaningfully identified (SE of x* = 1.45 log points).

The defensible conclusion is therefore twofold. There is no evidence of an inverted-U EKC in any specification. Equally, the evidence is insufficient to establish a statistically significant U-shape, because both the curvature and the endpoint slopes are insignificant. Under the decision rule of Section 2.7, H1 is not supported. Because this is a finding of non-detection, it is reported as “no evidence of an inverted U” rather than as a rejection of the EKC as an economic mechanism.

4.5 The first-difference model and diagnostics

Because H2 is not supported, Table 8 reports the first-difference model in Equation 5, the specification that does not rely on a levels relationship. Income growth has no statistically detectable short-run association with emissions growth. The coefficients are 0.129 (p = 0.706) for Δx and 0.054 (p = 0.936) for Δx2, and the two are jointly insignificant (p = 0.928). The energy-growth coefficient is positive but imprecise (0.331, p = 0.547). The renewable-share coefficient is large and significant (−1.211, p < 0.001), but it is identified almost entirely by 2 years, 2020 and 2022, in which the renewable share rose while emissions fell. In 2020 the fall coincided with the pandemic contraction. With a 2020 pulse dummy, the coefficient is −1.035 and is no longer significant at the 5% level (p = 0.059). Because the renewable share never exceeded 0.16% in the sample, this coefficient is interpreted as a statistical association, not as a causal effect of renewable deployment. The first-difference model passes all diagnostic tests (Table 9).

Table 9 reports the diagnostic tests for all dynamic models. The first-difference model shows no residual serial correlation at one or two lags (Breusch–Godfrey F p = 0.799 and 0.881), no ARCH effects, no departure from normality and no RESET-type misspecification. The levels-based ARDL and NARDL models show first-order residual autocorrelation that is significant or borderline. For the preferred ARDL, the Breusch–Godfrey test with one lag gives LM = 5.11 (p = 0.024) and F = 4.34 (p = 0.049). For the common-lag ARDL, the corresponding values are p = 0.040 and p = 0.100, while the two-lag test does not reject (F p = 0.267). First-order serial correlation is therefore not fully eliminated in the levels models. Three steps address it. First, all long-run p-values are also reported with HAC standard errors (Table 6), and the substantive conclusions are unchanged: the only coefficient that becomes significant, REN in the preferred model (HAC p = 0.042), is not significant in the common-lag model (p = 0.547). Second, the bounds test was repeated for the best-fitting lag configuration that is free of serial correlation, ARDL (1,0,0,0,0) (Breusch–Godfrey F p = 0.368 at one lag and 0.357 at two lags; ARCH p = 0.563; Jarque–Bera p = 0.566; RESET F (1, 24) = 0.74, p = 0.400), and its F-statistic of 1.17 is also below the I (0) bound (Table 5, row (j)). Third, the preferred inferential model for short-run effects is the first-difference specification, which passes all diagnostics. The RESET test does not reject in any model; this is reported as “no evidence of RESET-type functional-form misspecification at the 5% level” rather than as evidence of correct specification. The CUSUM and CUSUM-of-squares statistics remain within their 5% bounds for the preferred ARDL (Figure 4) and for the common-lag ARDL (Table 9).

4.6 Asymmetry, DOLS, structural breaks and omitted structural variables

4.6.1 Asymmetry (H3)

Table 10 reports the NARDL estimates. The NARDL bounds F-statistic (1.70) is below the I (0) bound, so the asymmetric model does not establish a levels relationship either. The conditional long-run coefficients are −0.299 for income increases (SE 0.738, p = 0.690; 95% interval −1.84 to 1.24) and −2.045 for income decreases (SE 4.038, p = 0.618; 95% interval −10.47 to 6.38). The error-correction coefficient is φ = −0.413 (SE 0.172, t = −2.40, conventional p = 0.026). It is negative, as stability of Equation 7 requires, and its bounds interpretation is the same as in Section 4.3. The Wald test does not reject long-run symmetry (θ+ = θ−: F (1, 20) = 0.25, p = 0.624; delta-method test of λ+ = λ−: χ2 (1) = 0.26, p = 0.608) or impact symmetry (F = 0.05, p = 0.830). Figure 5 plots the cumulative multipliers. The 90% Monte Carlo band (a conventional width for dynamic-multiplier bands) for the asymmetry curve contains zero at every horizon from 0 to 10 years. The appropriate conclusion is that no long-run asymmetry is detected under the reported NARDL test. Because the long-run framework is itself not supported by the bounds test, this is a statement about the absence of detectable asymmetry, not evidence of a symmetric equilibrium response.

4.6.2 DOLS

Table 11 (upper panel) reports DOLS estimates with one lead and one lag of the differenced regressors. In specification A (income and energy), the quadratic term is positive (1.343, p = 0.189) and the income terms are jointly insignificant (p = 0.396). In specification B, which adds REN, the quadratic coefficient turns negative (−1.848, p = 0.366), and none of the coefficients is significant. The renewable-share coefficient is unstable (−46.97, SE 31.05), which reflects the near-zero variation of REN over most of the sample. With two-sided HAC inference, a finite-sample correction and the t distribution, the quadratic term in specification A is not significant (p = 0.189). Without the finite-sample correction and with normal critical values, its p-value would be 0.069, which would not constitute conventional significance either. Since DOLS presupposes cointegration, these estimates are not evidence of a long-run equilibrium. They show only that the lack of a significant inverted U does not depend on the estimator, and that even the sign of the curvature is not robust.

4.6.3 Structural breaks

Level-shift dummies for 2014 and 2016 are individually and jointly insignificant in the preferred ARDL (joint F = 0.04, p = 0.964) and in the common-lag ARDL (joint F = 0.09, p = 0.916). The bounds statistic remains below the I (0) bound when they are included (Table 5). The Zivot–Andrews tests locate the most likely breaks endogenously: a level shift from 1997 for lnCO2, which rejects the unit root; from 2004 for lnGDP; and from 2008 for lnEN. Neither of the latter two rejects the unit root. The Gregory–Hansen test, which allows a level shift at an unknown date in the cointegrating regression, gives ADF* = −5.33 with a shift from 1996. This is well short of the simulated 10% critical value (−6.14), so no cointegration is detected even when a regime shift is allowed. The break dates selected by the data are in the late 1990s and the 2000s, not in 2014 or 2016. Within this sample, no shift associated with the 2014 oil-price collapse or the launch of Vision 2030 is detected in the per capita emissions process or in the conditional error-correction model. The carbon-intensity ratio does show a change after 2016 when that break date is imposed (Section 4.7), but the change is a slowdown of its decline.

4.6.4 Omitted structural variables

Adding log oil rents (lnOR, I (1) by ADF and PP) to the preferred model does not restore a levels relationship (F = 1.48, n = 30). The oil-rent coefficient is insignificant (λ = 0.149, p = 0.389), and first-order residual autocorrelation persists (Breusch–Godfrey χ2 (1) p = 0.013). Adding trade openness as well gives F = 1.24, with insignificant coefficients on both lnOR (p = 0.926) and lnTR (p = 0.463). The correlation between the baseline ARDL residuals and lnOR is 0.11. These results do not support the view that the residual autocorrelation reflects omitted rent variables. Residual autocorrelation is consistent with omitted dynamics or omitted variables in general, but in this sample oil rents and trade openness do not account for it.

4.7 Decoupling during the vision 2030 period

Table 12 reports the decoupling metrics defined in Equations 9 and 10E. For total emissions and total real GDP, every sub-period since 1990 shows weak (relative) decoupling, with Tapio elasticities between 0.34 and 0.63. For 2016–2022 total emissions rose by 4.0% while real GDP rose by 11.9% (ε = 0.34). Absolute decoupling of total emissions is not observed in any sub-period, and in the descriptive extension total emissions rose by 7.9% between 2016 and 2024. In per capita terms, the elasticities for 2010–2016 and 2016–2022 are negative (“strong decoupling” in Tapio’s classification), because per capita emissions fell between 2010 (22.09 t) and 2016 (20.87 t) and were slightly lower in 2022 (20.73 t) than in 2016. This classification depends on the end points: per capita emissions reached a post-2016 high of 23.25 t in 2019, and they fell by 2.4% between 2016 and 2024. Carbon intensity fell from 0.79 kg CO2 per 2011 Int$ in 1990 to 0.39 in 2016 and 0.37 in 2022 (Supplementary Appendix Figure A1). The segmented-trend model shows that the decline slowed after 2016 rather than accelerating. The pre-2016 trend is −3.3% per year (κ1 = −0.033, p < 0.001), and the post-2016 change is +3.0 percentage points per year (κ2 = 0.030, p < 0.001), so the post-2016 trend is close to zero. The level shift in 2016 is κ3 = 0.089 (p = 0.009). The post-2016 window contains only seven observations, so these estimates should be read as descriptive rather than structural.

H4 is therefore not supported in its absolute form. Total emissions continued to rise, more slowly than GDP, over the Vision 2030 period. The relative decoupling observed after 2016 continues a pattern visible since 1990 and did not accelerate. The analysis contains no policy-treatment variable or counterfactual, so these patterns are described as observed over the period and are not attributed to Vision 2030, either as a success or as a failure. Figure 6 shows that the renewable share remained below 1% of primary energy throughout, including in the descriptive years 2023–2024.

5 Discussion

5.1 What the evidence shows

The empirical findings can be stated without reference to any mechanism. Per-capita CO2 emissions in Saudi Arabia are high and bounded. After a level shift in the late 1990s they are stationary around a mean of about 20 t (sample mean 20.33 t; Table 3), whereas real income per capita grew by about 160% and follows an I (1) process. A series of this kind cannot share a common stochastic trend with income. Accordingly, the bounds test provides no evidence of a levels relationship in any of the 162 lag configurations or in the preferred model augmented with break dummies or with oil rents and trade openness, and the Gregory–Hansen test finds none when a regime shift is allowed. Consistent with this result, neither the long-run nor the short-run income terms are significant, there is no evidence of an inverted U, the curvature is not robust in sign across estimators, and income effects show no detectable asymmetry. Total emissions decoupled from GDP only in relative terms, and the decline in carbon intensity slowed after 2016.

These results agree with the majority of the Saudi ARDL literature in finding no support for an inverted U (Alshehry and Belloumi, 2017; Samargandi, 2017; Raggad, 2018; Aldegheishem, 2024; Moustafa and Alomran, 2025). They differ from that literature on whether a stable long-run relationship exists. Several factors may explain the difference: most of these studies use total rather than per capita emissions and longer samples that include the rapid emissions growth of the 1970s and 1980s (Table 1); regressor sets differ (Aldegheishem, 2024, whose per capita sample is close to ours, uses air passengers and trade openness rather than energy use); and deterministic terms and the use of asymptotic critical values may also differ. Our results do not show that earlier long-run estimates are wrong. They show that, for 1990–2022, per capita data and the present set of regressors, a levels relationship cannot be established once finite-sample critical values and the stationarity of emissions are taken into account. The same caution applies to the asymmetry literature. NARDL studies report that positive income shocks raise emissions more than negative shocks lower them (Raggad, 2020), that renewable and emissions shocks transmit differently (Toumi and Toumi, 2019), or that recent positive growth shocks reduced emissions (Moustafa and Alomran, 2025). In samples of 25–55 annual observations, asymmetries are estimated with wide confidence bands, as Figure 5 shows, and international NARDL evidence is similarly heterogeneous (Hammoudeh et al., 2015; Malik et al., 2020; Fatima et al., 2021; Mujtaba and Jena, 2021; Sreenu, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). The present failure to detect asymmetry is not inconsistent with earlier findings of asymmetry; it illustrates how imprecisely asymmetry is estimated in samples of this size.

The findings also connect to sector-level EKC evidence elsewhere. In South Africa’s transport sector, Oladunni et al. (2024) find support for the EKC hypothesis in a panel of the nine provinces, but all provinces remain on the rising segment and none has yet reached the turning point. Oladunni and Olanrewaju (2022) identify GDP and passenger vehicles as the main drivers of transport emissions in an extended STIRPAT panel. System-econometric studies of KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng likewise place fossil-energy use, urbanisation and passenger vehicles at the centre of emissions-mitigation analysis (Oladunni et al., 2025a; 2025b), which parallels the role of energy use as the most consistent proximate driver in the Saudi literature (Section 2.4). In these settings, as in Saudi Arabia, rising income has not yet been accompanied by falling emissions.

5.2 Possible mechanisms: the carbon curse and energy lock-in

The mechanisms discussed in this section are interpretations drawn from the wider literature. The model does not estimate them directly. The carbon-curse literature argues that rentier economies use resource rents to fund low domestic energy prices and public spending, which steers development towards energy-intensive sectors such as petrochemicals, desalination and cement (Dabboussi, 2024; Nwani et al., 2024; Okere et al., 2026). Threshold studies suggest that the curse operates once rents exceed a certain share of GDP (Nwani et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). On this reading, rising income expands an existing carbon-intensive structure rather than inducing the compositional and technological change that an EKC turning point requires. This is consistent with emissions per capita that are high but stable, and with income terms that have no detectable effect. However, the direct test in Section 4.6 finds no evidence that oil rents restore a levels relationship or explain the residual autocorrelation in this sample. The carbon-curse account is therefore one possible interpretation of the bounded emissions path. It is not a finding of this paper, and the residual autocorrelation should not be read as evidence of omitted rent effects.

5.3 Implications for decoupling and policy

The policy implications are conditional on the evidence. The model shows that income growth over 1990–2022 was not accompanied by any detectable income-related change in per capita emissions, and that total emissions decoupled only in relative terms. It does not show what effect Vision 2030 has had, because it contains no policy-treatment variable, the period from 2016 to 2022 has only seven income-matched observations, and no counterfactual is identified. Claims that Vision 2030 has had either a large or a negligible effect on emissions would go beyond the evidence.

Within these limits, three implications follow from combining the empirical results with the wider literature. First, because the data show no detectable tendency for income growth by itself to reduce emissions, decarbonisation is likely to require deliberate changes in the carbon intensity of energy and the energy intensity of output. These are the channels through which energy consumption links growth to emissions (Gershon et al., 2024), and the decoupling literature shows that absolute decoupling has been achieved only gradually and in a minority of economies (Haberl et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021; Hubacek et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; González-Álvarez and Montañés, 2023). Second, the renewable share, at 0.73% of primary energy in 2024, is still too small for its estimated coefficient to be interpreted economically (Section 4.5). Scaling renewable capacity and continuing energy-price reform (Al-Gahtani, 2024; Muneer et al., 2025; Selim and Alshareef, 2025) are therefore likely to be necessary for any future decoupling that the data could register. Third, the literature on finance and trade suggests that directing financial deepening and export strategy towards low-carbon activities could reduce the carbon intensity of growth (Ali et al., 2019; Shoaib et al., 2020; Udeagha and Breitenbach, 2023; Zhou et al., 2025). These are implications for policy design, not results estimated in this paper.

6 Conclusion

This paper asked whether an inverted-U EKC describes the relationship between income and per capita CO2 emissions in Saudi Arabia over 1990–2022, and whether a stable long-run relationship links emissions, income, energy use and the renewable share. The strongest defensible results are as follows. First, there is no statistical evidence of an inverted-U EKC in any reported specification, and the evidence is also insufficient to establish a statistically significant U-shape. Second, the ARDL bounds test provides no evidence of a stable long-run levels relationship. The F-statistic of 2.01 is below the I (0) bound under both asymptotic and finite-sample critical values, the bounds t-test is at most inconclusive at the 10% level, and the same conclusion holds across all 162 configurations in the pre-specified lag grid, in the best-fitting configuration free of serial correlation, with structural-break dummies, with a Gregory–Hansen regime shift and with oil rents and trade openness added; only one specification outside the pre-specified grid enters the inconclusive band. Third, per capita emissions are stationary around a shifting mean while income is I (1). This is consistent with the absence of a common trend and implies that a negative error-correction coefficient should not be read as equilibrium adjustment. Fourth, no long-run income asymmetry is detected, a result conditional on a long-run framework that the bounds test does not support. Fifth, total emissions show relative but not absolute decoupling from GDP after 2016, and the decline in carbon intensity slowed rather than accelerated. These patterns are not attributed causally to Vision 2030.

These conclusions are subject to several sources of uncertainty. The estimation sample has only 31 effective observations, so the bounds, asymmetry and trend-break tests have low power, and the null results should be read as “not detected in these data” rather than “shown not to exist”. The preferred levels ARDL and the NARDL retain first-order residual autocorrelation; HAC inference, the serial-correlation-free configuration in Table 5 and the first-difference model mitigate but do not remove this concern. The renewable share varies too little to support an economic interpretation of its coefficient. The analysis covers only seven observations with matched income data from 2016 to 2022.

Future research can address these limitations in several ways. Harmonised income data for 2023 onwards would allow re-estimation, and longer annual spans and sector-level data would increase the information available. Bootstrap ARDL tests (McNown et al., 2018) and Fourier-type cointegration procedures suited to oil-cycle economies could be applied. A panel of Gulf Cooperation Council members would test whether bounded per capita emissions and the absence of a levels relationship are shared across hydrocarbon exporters. Assessing Vision 2030 itself would require an explicit policy-evaluation design, for example, a synthetic-control or interrupted time-series approach with a defined treatment.
